A lot of creators get stuck because they're too busy creating this one type of content.

They create the kind of content that's designed to get the most views and engagement.

It’s kind of addicting. It’s nice to see the views and likes. It feeds your ego a bit.

But is it really moving the needle in your business?

If you wanna generate more sales, you need different types of content, and this content likely won’t get as many views as you’re used to.

This is called “middle of funnel” and “bottom of funnel” content.

Middle of funnel content is designed to build trust and establish a relationship with your audience, and also demonstrate your competence so people know you can actually help them.

Bottom of funnel is designed to generate leads and sales with more direct calls to action. This content usually gets the least views but drives the most revenue.

I find that most creators are usually lacking in one of the key types of content. They’re either creating too much TOF content and not enough MOF and BOF. Or they’re creating too much BOF (direct offers, too promotional and pitchy) but not enough TOF content that would get their message out to way more people.

Just something to keep in mind.

Hope this helps,
Beau

Skip senior leaders.

Advice gets replies.
Referral requests get ignored.

Many European startups quietly hire contributors.

• bug fix

• issue discussion

You become familiar before applying.

Search smarter.

Europe hires slower.

Recruiters aren’t the only gatekeepers.

Target:

You bypass crowded HR pipelines.

Study one hiring niche.

You sound informed, not desperate.

analysis.transcript: [slide 1] LACK OF DESIGN DESTROYS YOUR BUSINESS. TALKING THROUGH REAL BRAND EXAMPLES. ELECTROFORMA. [slide 2] ISSUE. Most companies bring designers in at the end of the business development process. The product and strategy were built, now it's time to make a wrap. The result of this can be the most expensive marketing mistake. [slide 3] APPLE. In 1997, Apple was 90 days away from bankruptcy. The losses exceeded $1B. At this point, Jobs putted design at the center of his product strategy. The iMac G3 was released in 1998. In the first 6 weeks, 800,000 units were sold, the company was saved. CASE STUDY. [slide 4] OATLY. In 2012, Oatly was a Swedish company with a nice product and zero recognition. New creative director John Schoolcraft rewrote the packaging by hand with plain, human language. Three years later, there were queues in stores and shortages in Europe. The text on packages became the main sales channel. CASE STUDY. [slide 5] HERMÈS. Hermès spends only 4,5% percentage of its revenue on advertising. Its primary media channels are products, storefronts, packages, and the signature orange color recognized around the world. Over 180 years, visual consistency has preserved millions in marketing spend. CASE STUDY. [slide 6] TARGET. In the 2000s, Target tried competing with Walmart on price and lost. The solution was to make design a competitive advantage for the mass market: designer collaborations, distinctive private-label products. Target stopped competing on price. It started competing on meaning, turning a routine shopping into an experience people actually enjoyed. CASE STUDY. [slide 7] THE MECHANISM IS MEASURED IN REVENUE. TRUST: Visual consistency reduces buyer uncertainty. PRICE: Products appear more valuable and can command higher margins. LOYALTY: Recognition lowers the cost of customer comeback. [slide 8] WHEN DO YOU FIRST INVOLVE A DESIGNER? When the product is already finished? OR When has the first strategic decision not been made yet? THE ANSWER DETERMINES WHETHER DESIGN IS ONE OF THE MAIN REASONS PEOPLE BUY OR JUST A NON-INFLUENCING WRAPPER. [slide 9] COMPANIES THAT THINK THROUGH DESIGN FROM DAY ONE DON'T SPEND MORE ON DESIGN, THEY SIMPLY SPEND ONCE. ELECTROFORMA. BUREAU OF BUSINESS DESIGN.

1. Target the right companies

Not every Parisian company is built to hire internationals. Go straight to multinationals, tech startups, and scale-ups — they have the HR infrastructure and visa experience to actually bring you on board.

Paris runs on relationships. One conversation at a startup apéro or expat meetup can unlock doors that 100 cold applications never will. Show up in person whenever you can.

EU citizen? You’re free to go. Non-EU? Know your options cold — talent passport, work permit, company sponsorship. Bring it up confidently, not apologetically. It signals you’re serious.

1 page. Clean. Often includes a photo. Lead with impact, not job duties. French hiring managers read fast — make every line count.

→ Welcome to the Jungle (international-friendly)

→ LinkedIn (localize your headline to Paris)

→ Relocate.me (visa-sponsored roles)

→ EuroJobs.com
6. Patience is part of the process

3-month hiring timelines are normal here. Follow up once. Stay warm. Don’t ghost — Paris is a small world.

analysis.summary: A side-by-side comparison of six different AI video generation tools (Runway 4, Seedance, Higgsfield, Google VEO, Kling 2.5, and Minimax) using the same 'distracted boyfriend' meme prompt.
tips: Different AI video models interpret complex character interactions and meme-based prompts with varying degrees of success.
Evaluate AI video tools based on their ability to maintain character consistency and logical movement within a scene.

concepts.explanation: The process of using machine learning models to create video content from text or image prompts.

analysis.transcript: [scene: A 2x3 grid of video clips showing the 'distracted boyfriend' meme being generated by different AI tools. The audio is a song with the lyrics 'Well when the sun goes down and the moon comes up'.] [scene: Runway 4 shows the woman in red walking past the man.] [scene: Seedance shows the man turning his head.] [scene: Higgsfield shows the man turning his head.] [scene: Google VEO shows the man turning his head and a bus passing by.] [scene: Kling 2.5 shows the man turning his head.] [scene: Minimax shows the woman in red walking away.]

medium.caption:
I tested the distracted boyfriend meme across six AI video models to see how each interprets a simple human scenario.

Runway 4 looked clean and well-lit, but it felt frozen. The woman in red didn’t move, and the reactions lacked flow. It replicated the image, not the moment.

Seedance produced smooth motion but held the same shot for too long. It understood movement, not narrative. You could tell it needed more instruction to decide what happens next.

Higgsfield handled expressions really well — especially the girlfriend’s reaction — but the pacing was slightly off. It felt like it was processing emotions a frame behind.

Google VEO didn’t follow my prompt exactly, but it built its own logic. The girl walked up and hit him — unexpected, but contextually believable. It showed how some models start to infer intent rather than just follow orders.

Kling 2.5 stayed closest to the source image and rendered motion accurately. But it struggled with timing and character interaction. It could animate a scene but not sustain it.

Minimax technically broke the most, but what it did was still interesting. The girl running off wasn’t right, but it showed unpredictability — almost like the model overreacted to the situation.

What’s clear is that these tools don’t just vary in output — they vary in interpretation. Some replicate, some predict, and a few attempt to understand.

What are your thoughts? Who do you think did the best job with it?? 👀 Let’s discuss in the comments.

analysis.summary: A step-by-step guide on creating a mixed-media poster effect in Photoshop using texture overlays, print simulation plugins, and layer styles.

resources.name: PrintMachine
resources.purpose: Photoshop plugin for creating print, scan, and ink bleed effects.

workflow_steps: Set up a 16x20 inch, 300 dpi, 16-bit Photoshop document.
Add paper and print textures to the image using specific blend modes (Screen, Soft Light, Overlay).
Merge layers and use the PrintMachine plugin to apply print and scanned looks.
Re-apply the print effect to the original layer, enable ink bleed, and merge the resulting layers.
Place masking tape PNGs, merge them, and clip the ink bleed layer to the tape.
Duplicate the tape layer, move it on top, and adjust blend modes/opacity with a drop shadow.
Place cutout images on a new layer with a white background and apply the print effect.
Mask out cutouts and apply specific Bevel & Emboss and Drop Shadow layer styles.
Use the Rectangular Marquee tool to select parts of the main image and move them to a new layer.
Use Edit > Transform > Warp to add curvature to cutouts and apply layer styles.
Add a Levels adjustment layer to enhance black values.
tips: Use 16-bit documents for the best results when applying ink bleed effects.
Rename your layers consistently (e.g., 'DIGITAL PRINT', 'INK FADE') to keep track of the process.
Use the Warp tool on cutouts to add depth and a tactile, physical feel to the composition.
Apply a drop shadow to masking tape elements to make them appear as if they are physically sitting on top of the poster.

concepts.explanation: A design style that combines different visual elements like photography, textures, and physical objects to create a layered, collage-like aesthetic.

Mistral's 7B model serves a million-token chat on hardware that should choke at thirty thousand. The trick isn't in the parameters. It's sliding window attention.

Normal attention lets every token look back at every prior token. The KV cache grows with the conversation. A million tokens means a million tokens of cache — and that's what should be unaffordable on small hardware.

Sliding window attention caps the lookback. Each token only attends to the last few thousand tokens (Mistral 7B uses 4K). As new tokens arrive, the window slides forward and old tokens fall out of view. The cache stops growing past the window size, so memory becomes flat instead of linear. About 4K tokens of memory, no matter how long the conversation runs.

The catch: the window is positional, not semantic. The model can't see anything that falls outside the last 4K tokens — it doesn't matter what those older tokens contained, they're invisible. So when an inference provider advertises native long context on a tiny model, you're seeing sliding window math, not magic.

The fix when you actually need far-back context: pair sliding window with attention sinks (StreamingLLM keeps the first few tokens pinned as overflow drains) or pull the older context explicitly with RAG. Don't trust the window to remember what it can't physically reach.

Sliding window keeps memory flat. Past the window, you need RAG.

Reverse engineering looks like magic until you see the toolkit behind it.

Every cracked thing, every malware breakdown, every "how does this actually work" answer starts with the same handful of tools. They take a compiled binary, something that looks like pure noise, and turn it back into something you can read, trace, and understand.

Here are 7 that real reverse engineers reach for, and what each one is actually good at:

Ghidra → the NSA's free suite. Decompiles raw machine code back into readable C-style pseudocode.

radare2 → the scriptable command-line framework. Analyze, disassemble, and patch, all from the terminal.

x64dbg → the open-source standard for debugging Windows binaries. Step through code and watch registers live.

GDB → Linux debugging with a context dashboard showing registers, disassembly, and breakpoints at every stop.

Frida → dynamic instrumentation. Hook functions in a running process and rewrite return values on the fly.

Cheat Engine → memory scanner and live patcher. Find and freeze values in a running process.

ImHex → a modern hex editor built for RE, with a pattern language and a visual node graph for decoding data.

You don't need all 7 on day one. Pick the one that matches what you're pulling apart: a Windows app, a Linux binary, a mobile target, or a raw file you've never seen before.

Save this so you have the map next time a binary lands on your desk.

🇫🇷 There’s a French pension account that legally lets you withdraw money early — to buy your main home.

PER stands for Plan d’Épargne Retraite. It’s a retirement savings account open to any adult living in France — salaried, self-employed, or neither. You contribute what you want, when you want.

THE TAX BENEFIT

Every euro you put in can reduce your taxable income in France. The annual ceiling for a salaried employee: up to €37,680 off your taxable base.

If you’re paying 30–41% income tax, the math is significant.

The money is locked until retirement — with one major exception.

If you’re buying your résidence principale in France — your primary home, not a second property — you can withdraw your PER funds early. No penalty. Fully legal. The tax treatment depends on whether your contributions were deducted when paid in.

Which means: you get the tax deduction now, the money grows, and when you’re ready to buy in France, you can access it.

ONE CHOICE THAT MATTERS

When you contribute, you decide: take the tax deduction now, or skip it.

→ Deduct now → tax on the capital when you withdraw at retirement (or for home purchase)
→ Don’t deduct → your capital comes out clean; only the gains are taxed

The right choice depends on your current tax bracket and your plan for the money.

If you’re American: PER can work, but the type of account and underlying investments matter — requires coordination with a US tax specialist.

This is one of those products that exists, works exactly as described, and most expats in France have never heard of it.

If your AI portraits feel fake, here’s why..
It’s not the tool. It’s the training data.

AI learned how to see faces through social media and stock photography.

Millions of images where people are already performing for the camera

posed, polished, aware they’re being watched.

the moment awareness kills authenticity.

That’s how you make your portraits feel human.
